'''Lalbhai Dalpatbhai''' (1863-1912)<ref name=x>Business World -1987 - Volume 7 - Page 44</ref> was an industrialist and one of the first generation [[textile mill]] owners from [[Ahmedabad]], who laid the foundation of the present-day Lalbhai group<ref>{{cite news|title=Lalbhai group poised for major expansion and diversification spree|url=https://www.indiatoday.in/magazine/economy/story/19880515-lalbhai-group-poised-for-major-expansion-and-diversification-spree-798235-1988-05-14|access-date=28 February 2014|newspaper=India Today|date=15 May 1988}}</ref>  of Industries.

==Life==
Lalbhai was born in 1863 at Ahmedabad to Dalpatbhai Bhagubhai in a Gujarati [[Oswal]] [[Gujarati Jains|Jain]] family of ''[[sahukar|nagarsheths]]'' and jewellers and was a direct descendant of the 16th-century merchant, [[Shantidas Jhaveri]].<ref name=a>{{cite book |title=The politics of textiles: the Indian cotton-mill industry and the legacy of Swadeshi, 1900-1985 |first=Simon Robert Brough |last=Leadbeater |year=1993 |page=69 |publisher=SAGE |isbn=978-8-17036-296-8}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kalia |first=Ravi |title=Gandhinagar: Building National Identity in Postcolonial India |publisher=University of South Carolina Press |year=2004 |pages=45}}</ref> He was the great grandson of Vakhatchand's second son, Motibhai.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Tripathi |first1=Dwijendra |title=Business Houses in Western India: A Study in Entrepreneurial Response, 1850-1956 |last2=Mehta |first2=Makrand |publisher=South Asia Publications |year=1990 |pages=89}}</ref>

After growing up, he carried on the traditional business of precious gems of his family. His father Dalpatbhai Bhagubhai was also in cotton trading business since the 1870<ref name=p>Piramal, Gita. Business Legends. p. 309.</ref> As an expansion of his cotton trading business, he decided to start his own cotton mill and in 1896 he floated the Saraspur Mills followed by Raipur Mills in 1897.<ref>Education and the Disprivileged: Nineteenth and Twentieth ...by Sabyasachi Bhattacharya - 2002</ref><ref name=a/> These two mills laid the foundation of present-day Lalbhai group.<ref name=p/> The group was later expanded by his sons and noted nationalist and philanthropist, [[Kasturbhai Lalbhai]], Narottambhai Lalbhai, Chimanbhai Lalbhai and grandsons like [[Shrenik Kasturbhai Lalbhai]], [[Arvind Narottambhai Lalbhai]] and [[Chinubhai Chimanbhai]]. The group now consists of mills like [[Arvind Mills]], [[Atul Limited]] among others.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.atul.co.in/about_us/heritage_lalbhaifamily.html |title=Lalbhai Family |access-date=28 February 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150218165327/http://www.atul.co.in/about_us/heritage_lalbhaifamily.html |archive-date=18 February 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

For most of his life Lalbhai lived in his ancestral home in Jhaveriwad in the [[Historic City of Ahmadabad|walled city of Ahmedabad]]. Forty family members shared an eight-room home along with a dozen servants. Between 1910 and 1912 he moved into a newly constructed colonial style mansion in [[Shahibaug]]. He was a strict father and the family had a simple and traditional style of living.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Piramal |first=Gita |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pAltAwAAQBAJ&dq=lalbhai+dalpatbhai&pg=RA1-PT257 |title=Business Legends |publisher=Penguin Books |year=2010|isbn=978-93-5118-148-4 }}</ref>

He died in 1912 at the age of 49 due to a heart attack. Perimal notes that Lalbhai had been stressed due to a recent acrimonious family dispute involving division of family property and businesses.<ref name="x" /><ref name="p" /><ref name=":0" />
